cues.text: A Council Amid a Vulgate in Progress
In 382, Pope Damasus I convened a synod at Rome during the same years he commissioned the scholar St. Jerome to begin revising the Latin Bible.
That revision would eventually grow into the Vulgate, a coincidence of timing that later historians have long connected to the council's business.
The council addressed the question Jerome's translation work presupposed: which books belonged, with full authority, to Sacred Scripture.
The Damasine List
Among the acts attributed to this council is a document scholars call the Damasine List , a catalogue enumerating the books of both Testaments.
The Roman Church recognized these books as canonical, and its twenty-seven New Testament titles correspond almost exactly to the canon Catholics and most other Christians recognize today.

The list's precise date, authorship, and even its formal attachment to this particular synod remain genuinely debated among modern scholars, since the fullest surviving text comes down through later manuscript transmission rather than a single, uncontested contemporary record.
A Church Defining Its Own Scriptures
Whatever the precise circumstances of its promulgation, the Damasine List reflects a broader, ongoing process across the fourth-century Church.
This process settled which circulating Christian writings belonged to the inspired canon and which, however edifying, did not.
It would be echoed and reinforced within the following two decades by regional African councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397), which issued closely similar lists of their own.
Damasus and the Authority of Rome
The council also fits within Damasus's broader pontificate-long project of asserting Rome's primacy among the churches.

During this period, the pope worked to distinguish the authoritative teaching of the apostolic see of Peter from claims by Constantinople and other Eastern sees jockeying for precedence after the previous year's Council of Constantinople.
A council settling, with Roman authority, the very boundaries of the Scriptures the whole Church read fit naturally within that larger ambition.
Legacy

Though the Council of Rome left a far thinner historical footprint than the great ecumenical councils of the same century, its association with the Damasine List gives it quiet but genuine significance.
In the Bible's formation, few councils, however modest their surviving record, have shaped every subsequent Christian's encounter with Scripture so directly as this one gathering in Rome.
It was convened in the very years the Church's greatest biblical scholar was at work turning that same settled canon into the Latin text the West would read for the next fifteen centuries.
